entities.summary:
Chartres Cathedral (Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Chartres) is widely considered the finest example of French High Gothic architecture, built primarily between 1194 and 1220 CE in Chartres, France, 80 kilometers southwest of Paris. A UNESCO World Heritage site, it is renowned for its extraordinary medieval stained glass — 176 windows covering 2,600 square meters — which remain among the best-preserved in the world, including the famous 'Chartres blue' glass.

The cathedral stands on a site of pre-Christian sacred significance: a well in the crypt venerated since Druidic times, and a small statue of Notre Dame de Sous-Terre (Our Lady Below the Earth) considered miraculous. The Sancta Camisia — the robe allegedly worn by the Virgin Mary when she gave birth to Jesus — was the cathedral's most precious relic, donated by Charlemagne and drawing pilgrims from across Europe. When the previous cathedral burned in 1194, the survival of the relic was seen as a miracle mandating rebuilding.

Chartres pioneered Gothic architectural innovations: pointed arches, flying buttresses, ribbed vaulting, and large windows that flooded interiors with light representing divine illumination. The cathedral's two contrasting spires — the south Romanesque (1145) and north Flamboyant Gothic (1513) — have become a symbol of how medieval builders added to structures across centuries. Rodin called Chartres 'the Acropolis of France.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Chartres Cathedral is the supreme achievement of Gothic architecture, its stained glass creating Europe's most complete medieval visual program and its innovations influencing church building across the continent for centuries.
